tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

Nothing 288 inside the checkout is reclaimed automatically; `scripts/sdd-state prune --repo

` 289 lists and removes idle plan directories only when asked. Read the 328 plan's `**Spec:**` header and the spec file it names: the spec is the 329 binding authority the plan argues from, and conflicts inside the plan 330 resolve against it. A plan whose spec is `none` or unreachable gets a 331 ledger line saying so — without a spec, a conflict has no tiebreaker but 332 your human partner. 333 334 When the plan has a spec, dry-run the decision compiler over it now: 335 `bash /scripts/decisions-compile --dry-run` 336 (the finishing-a-development-branch skill, `../finishing-a-development-branch/` 337 relative to this one). Exit 0 confirms the spec's `## Decisions` list parses; 338 its numbered listing goes into the ledger under a `Decisions listing:` line 339 for the extractor's dispatch. Exit 2 for a missing list is the legacy-spec 340 case: draft the list from the spec's own text, one item per decision it 341 states, show it to your human partner, and write it into the spec once they 342 approve it, committing that edit on the branch. Any other exit 2 names what 343 to fix first (a spec that is not committed, or a `Supersedes:` problem) to 344 resolve with them the same way. After any repair, run the dry run again 345 until it exits 0, and only then write its numbered listing into the ledger. 346 The session is at its start, so this costs no cycle time. When the plan has 347 no spec (`none`, or unreachable, per the ledger line above), write 348 `Decisions: none (no spec)` in the ledger and skip the listing, the 349 extractor and the spec in the hand-off: finishing then takes its test-only 350 path. 351 352 Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts, writing down 353 what you checked as you check it: 354 355 - tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints 356 - anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a 357 defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block) 358 359 The scan's output is a table, not a verdict. One row for every pair of tasks 360 that share a file or an interface: the two tasks, what one produces against 361 what the other consumes, and what you found. One row for every task: whether 362 its own text agrees with itself — the tests it specifies against the code it 363 specifies, the files it creates against the files it later touches. "The scan 364 is clean" without those rows is not a scan you ran. 365 366 Write the table to the ledger. Then present everything it surfaced to your 367 human partner as ONE batched question — each finding beside the plan text 368 that mandates it, asking which governs — before execution begins, not one 369 interrupt per discovery mid-plan. Each finding is a decision with 370 consequences downstream, so it gets the shape the brainstorming skill's 371 Deciding Together section describes: the conflict and what each resolution 372 costs in chat, then the selection widget to collect the answers. If the scan 373 is clean, proceed without comment. The review loop remains the net for 374 conflicts that only emerge from implementation. 375 376 ## Model Selection 377 378 Match the model to the task's difficulty rather than defaulting. Two rules are 379 defaults you will get wrong by omission, so they stay here: **always specify 380 the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent** — an omitted model inherits 381 your session's, usually the most capable and most expensive — and **a mid-tier 382 model is the floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose 383 descriptions**, whatever the schedule pressure. The cheapest tier is for 384 transcription, where the task's own text carries the complete code to write, 385 and for single-file mechanical fixes. The per-role guidance, the complexity 386 signals, and the fix-loop escalation rule are in 387 [model-selection.md](model-selection.md). 388 389 ## The Task Loop 390 391 **Batch small same-shape work.** When the plan lists several tasks that are 392 each a small, independent edit of the same kind — the same one-line fix, 393 constant change, or field addition repeated across files — do not dispatch 394 one subagent per task. Compose ONE dispatch brief listing every file and 395 its change, send the whole batch to a single subagent, and review its diff 396 as one unit. Reserve one-dispatch-per-task for work that needs its own 397 judgment, its own tests, or its own review surface. 398 A batch's effective risk tier for the per-task Codex gate is the MAX of the 399 batched tasks' declared tiers — batching low-tier tasks never manufactures 400 a gate skip. 401 402 Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent 403 prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session 404 and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files. 405 406 **Waiting on subagents and long commands.** On Claude Code, wait in the foreground: 407 408 - Dispatch implementer, task-reviewer, fix-round, re-review and final-reviewer subagents with `run_in_background: false`. Your next step always depends on the result, and a foreground call keeps your turn open, which is what an editor such as Zed shows as the session working. A background dispatch ends the turn while the subagent runs, and the editor shows the session idle. 409 - Run a covering command expected to finish within 10 minutes in the foreground, with an explicit timeout of at least its expected runtime and at most 600000 ms. 410 - A command that may run past 10 minutes is a tracked job. Allocate it in the foreground with `scripts/tracked-job new PLAN_FILE --budget-ms ` (the watch budget below; the helper writes the `jobdir=` line in the ledger itself), launch `scripts/tracked-job run -- ` through the tracked background option with the budget as its timeout, then watch it in the foreground with repeated `scripts/tracked-job wait --max-ms 600000` calls: `exited code=0` is success; any other `exited` code is a failed command, handled as that command's failure (a failed test is a fix round, a failed covering command a failed task); `running` at the bound means another `wait`; on `lost`, run `tracked-job stop ` first and read its answer before you go on: only `stopped` or `not-running` means the survivors are swept and the job can be treated as failed (a process in the job's group that carried no fence is left alone and counted as `skipped` in `/meta.json`, and one that outlived the KILL is counted in `survivors`; report a nonzero `survivors` or `skipped`, or a record you cannot read, to your human partner with the jobdir and pgid before you go on, and never call that job stopped); `busy` means the lock was held and nothing was swept, so run `stop` again; `status=error` means the job directory could not be read, so escalate it to your human partner naming the jobdir and leave the job live; `lost-unswept pgid=` means the sweep needs a shell that can list processes and read their identity (the sandbox cannot), so the job stays live to the stop guard until `tracked-job stop ` runs where it can: report it to your human partner with its pgid beside the failure, and expect a reused pid to read as `running` until that sweep. When you need a job's output, write the tail of its `out.log` to `/reports/job-.txt` and cite the path; output never goes in the ledger. A background shell you start in a turn without `tracked-job` is live work no job record names: end the turn while one is still running and the stop guard refuses that turn end as `live-shell`. Codex reviews already follow this shape through the recipe's `status --wait --json` loop. 411 - **Watch budget.** The total watch on one job is three times the plan's stated runtime for it, or 60 minutes when the plan states none, capped at the harness's maximum background lifetime (7200000 ms on Claude Code). The watch ends when `wait` reports `exited`, `lost` or `lost-unswept`; a supervisor the harness killed writes no exit file, and `wait` reports it as `lost`. When the budget is spent with the job still running, run `tracked-job stop ` and read its answer before you end the turn: `stopped` or `not-running` means the job is over, so write the `out.log` tail to `/reports/job-.txt` and report BLOCKED naming that path (a nonzero `survivors` or `skipped` in `/meta.json`, or a record you cannot read, is reported the same way, with the jobdir and pgid, and that job is never called stopped); `busy` means the workspace lock was held and nothing changed, so run `stop` again; `stop-timeout` means the supervisor has not concluded the job, so run `stop` again, three calls in all, and escalate a third one to your human partner as a job still live, naming the jobdir; `status=error` means the job directory could not be read, so escalate it the same way, naming the jobdir; `lost-unswept pgid=` leaves the job live, so report it to your human partner as still live with its pgid, never as stopped. 412 413 On a harness whose subagents run asynchronously, never poll a wait interface with short timeouts, and never sit in one silent, open-ended wait either. While you have local work — ledger updates, packaging the next review, reading reports — keep working; child results arrive on their own. When you are genuinely idle, wait in bounded stretches (five to ten minutes, where your platform allows), and between stretches post one line of status and reconcile your live children: list them, and chase any that finished without reporting. A bounded stretch keeps nearly all of a long wait's efficiency while guaranteeing a stuck or lost child is noticed within minutes, not at the end of the session. Codex's `wait_agent` blocks inside the turn; `using-hyperpowers/references/codex-tools.md` maps it. 414 415 ### 1. Dispatch the implementer 416 417 Record BASE right after `git switch ` and before dispatching, as the 418 task branch's fork point from the integration branch: 419 `git merge-base HEAD refs/heads/` (the full ref name, so 420 a tag with the branch's name cannot be read instead). On a fresh claim that 421 is the claim's `from=` commit. On a takeover it is the original claim's base, 422 or, once the conflict route has merged the integration branch into the task 423 branch, the integration head merged in; the previous holder's commits stay in 424 the review package and the fix-round diffs either way, which both need BASE. 425 A HEAD read before the claim can lag the integration branch while other 426 sessions merge. 427 428 - **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's 429 `scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a 430 uniquely named file and prints `wrote : lines`. Take the path 431 from that line; do not paste the line itself into a dispatch. Compose the 432 dispatch so the 433 brief stays the single source of 434 requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this 435 task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this 436 first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim"; 437 (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot 438 know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief; 439 (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers, 440 magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never 441 make a subagent read the whole plan file. 442 - **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief 443 (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in 444 the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and 445 returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns. 446 - A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not 447 paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into 448 later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99% 449 was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it 450 touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else. 451 - The dispatch carries the no-subagents contract (it is in the 452 implementer template): the implementer never dispatches subagents — 453 not helpers, and never a reviewer. Review arrives from you, after the 454 report. In real sessions, every reviewer a worker spawned duplicated 455 the task review the controller dispatched anyway — a full extra 456 review seat per task. 457 - Subagents follow hyperpowers:test-driven-development for the task's tests. 458 - If an earlier task deferred a finding in the area this task touches — a 459 Minor in the ledger, or one your human partner decided — carry a pointer 460 to that ledger entry in the dispatch. 461 - Ask what to take: `scripts/sdd-state next PLAN_FILE --session `. 462 `status=next tasks=` names the claimable tasks in plan order, this 463 session's own claims first; claim the first: 464 `scripts/sdd-state claim PLAN_FILE N --session `. `claimed` prints the 465 task branch and its base: check the branch out (`git switch `) and 466 dispatch on it; `held` with your own session id (`own=1`, a resume after 467 compaction) prints the same two fields: check the branch out and proceed; 468 `held` with `own=1` and `merged=1` means the task is already merged and its 469 branch deleted: check nothing out and resume it at its completion line 470 (Complete the task, below); `claimed` with `takeover=1` and `merged=1` 471 means the same after a takeover: the task is already merged, so check 472 nothing out, dispatch nothing, and resume it at its completion line (the 473 previous holder's task branch may still exist; you do not need it); 474 `held` from `claim` after `next` offered the task is a race lost, run 475 `next` again; `blocked` means the plan moved under you, run `next` again. 476 A task held by another session is ordinary while next offers another: take 477 what it offers. Take a held task over only on your human partner's 484 explicit yes to a question that names the holder and the time since 485 (`--takeover`), recording the takeover beside the original identity; 486 `own-blocked` means an amendment put a prerequisite under your own claim: 487 post, print the board, hand back, and let your human partner remove the 488 edge or let the prerequisite complete. `done`, `no-workspace` and `error` 489 keep their handling: `done`: another session completed the task since you 490 read the ledger; read its completion line, mark the task done, and never 491 dispatch it. `no-workspace` (exit 2): the workspace is gone (finished or 492 pruned elsewhere); stop, run `sync`, and re-read the ledger before 493 anything else. `error` (exit 2, the same exit as `no-workspace` and a 494 different problem): a read or a write failed, and the claim may already 495 have been published; only your own retry of the same claim (which then 496 answers `held own=1`) or a takeover clears it. Stop, show the stderr line, 497 and retry the same claim once its cause is fixed; `sync` is still not the 498 answer. Any other status stops the dispatch until `claim` succeeds; show 499 its stderr line. 500 - Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result in the 501 ledger's task entry 502 (`Task : implementer (model , session , worktree , branch )`) — 503 fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent where the harness has no foreground 504 dispatch and dispatch on its recorded model where it does, and after compaction the ledger is 505 the only place the identity survives once its agent has exited. An 506 identity that was never written down forces a fresh takeover where a 507 resume was owed. 508 - When another session may be live on this plan, append ledger lines with a 509 quoted heredoc (`cat >> /progress.md <<'EOF'`), never with the 510 Edit tool, whose read-modify-write drops a line another session appended 511 in between. 512 - One implementer at a time in this session: parallel work is other sessions' (one controller per task branch); never dispatch two implementers at once here. 513 - Where the Agent tool offers `run_in_background`, dispatch with it false; where it does not (fork mode in an interactive terminal), dispatches run in the background and the stop guard treats them as live work. 514 515 Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md) 516 517 ### 2. Handle the report 518 519 **Subagent Reports Are Claims.** Subagent reports are claims, not 520 evidence. Before acting on any completed-status report (DONE or DONE_WITH_CONCERNS) or a fix report — 521 dispatching the reviewer, re-running a gate, marking a task complete — the 522 controller re-runs the named covering test command directly and compares 523 the output against the report. A misreported result is a failed task: 524 re-dispatch with the discrepancy named, not a bookkeeping correction. 525 526 Every implementer and fix dispatch names either its covering test 527 command(s) or an explicit `no covering command: ` line plus the 528 controller's substitute verification (read the diff against the brief; 529 render or grep the changed doc). A dispatch naming neither is malformed — 530 fix the dispatch, not the rule. 531 532 A covering command must be able to fail. One that can no-op on the state 533 under test — a changed-files linter on a clean tree, a test filter that 534 matches nothing — is not covering evidence, however honestly it exits 0. 535 Name the files or the test ids explicitly so the command exercises what 536 the report claims. 537 538 Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately: 539 540 **DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints `wrote : commit(s), bytes`, so take the path from that line; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task). If `review-package` exits non-zero, read its stderr and fix the range before dispatching — exit 2 means bad inputs (wrong argument count, a missing plan file, a ref that does not resolve) or an ancestry check git itself could not answer (a missing or corrupt object); exit 3 means BASE..HEAD is empty or HEAD is not a descendant of BASE, usually a wrong-branch commit; never dispatch a reviewer without a package. Otherwise, dispatch the task reviewer with the path. 541 542 **DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review. 543 544 **NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch. 545 546 **BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker: 547 1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model 548 2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model 549 3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces 550 4. If the plan itself is wrong, stop and escalate to your human partner — the plan text, what it breaks, and the correction you would make 551 552 **Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change. 553 554 If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer 555 clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't 556 rush it into implementation. 557 558 ### 3. Review the task 559 560 Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the 561 final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a 562 report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both 563 required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are 564 needed. Note the task's effective risk tier as you go (see Risk Tiers, 565 below) — the Claude task review always runs, but the tier decides whether 566 step 4's per-task Codex gate does. 567 568 - Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's 569 `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` — it prints 570 `wrote : commit(s), bytes`, so take the path from that line 571 and pass it to the reviewer (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, 572 `git diff --stat`, and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one 573 uniquely named file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees 574 the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read 575 call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer — 576 never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never 577 dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file. 578 - **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief 579 file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global 580 constraints that bind the task. Write those global constraints to a small 581 file alongside the brief and report: the per-task Codex gate takes the 582 same file as its global-constraints handoff. 583 - The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention 584 lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global 585 Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the 586 stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches 587 Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI, 588 test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS 589 project's spec demands. 590 - Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests 591 if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason 592 - Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the 593 same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence 594 - Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to 595 ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a 596 false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review 597 loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X 598 as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are 599 pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop. When the plan supplies 600 example code, weaknesses in that code are fair review targets — the example 601 was a starting point, not evidence that its weaknesses were chosen. 602 The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements 603 that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the 604 review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task 605 complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer 606 lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec 607 review — it enters the fix loop with the other findings. 608 609 Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md) 610 611 ### 4. The fix loop 612 613 The loop triggers when the review reports spec ❌, any Critical or Important 614 finding, a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real gap, or a blocking finding from 615 the per-task Codex gate below. 616 617 Task-reviewer findings are claims too. The fixing implementer verifies 618 each finding against the code before fixing it 619 (hyperpowers:receiving-code-review); a finding is declined only as 620 refuted or corrected with file:line evidence, which the controller 621 records in the ledger; a confirmed finding is fixed or carried open; a 622 finding nobody can settle stays open and counts against the round cap. 623 624 Before the loop starts, two routes leave it immediately: 625 626 - Record Minor findings in the progress ledger as you go 627 (`Task : minor (deferred): `), and point the final 628 whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed 629 before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard. Minor findings 630 never enter the loop. 631 - A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with what 632 the plan's text requires — is your human partner's decision: present the 633 finding and the plan text beside it and ask which governs. Do not dismiss 634 the finding because the plan mandates it, and do not dispatch a fix that 635 contradicts the plan without asking. 636 637 Everything else enters the loop — the Claude task reviewer's blocking 638 findings and the per-task Codex gate's blocking findings alike. They are ONE 639 loop with ONE shared cap of **five rounds per task**: the gate does not run 640 a count of its own. A fix round is one fix dispatch — or one 641 controller-applied de-minimis fix — plus one scoped re-review. 642 643 **Rounds 1-3 — the same model, carrying the task's record.** Where the Agent 644 tool offers `run_in_background` (Claude Code outside fork mode), dispatch a 645 fresh implementer in the foreground (`run_in_background: false`) with the 646 brief path, the report-file path, and the open findings verbatim, on the 647 original implementer's model (the `model` in its ledger identity line); 648 tell it a prior implementer did the 649 task and the report file records what it did and tried. A foreground 650 dispatch keeps your turn open until the fix returns, so a fix round on 651 Claude Code dispatches a fresh foreground implementer; a SendMessage resume 652 is for harnesses without the option, Claude Code's fork mode among them. On 653 those harnesses, resume the original 654 implementer with the findings verbatim: its context is intact. If the 655 harness cannot message a live subagent either, dispatch a fresh implementer 656 with the brief path, the report-file path, and the findings; the report file 657 is the persistent memory either way. 658 659 **Rounds 4-5 — dispatch a fresh takeover implementer on a more capable 660 model** (per Model Selection), with the brief path, the report-file path, 661 the open findings, and this framing: "A prior implementer attempted this 662 task [N] times; you own it now. Read the report file for what was tried." A 663 loop that survives three rounds usually means the same model cannot see 664 its own problem: the takeover brings a more capable one. 665 666 **Every round, either way:** the implementer fixes, re-runs the tests 667 covering the amended code, appends its fix report to the same report file, 668 and returns the short contract. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm 669 the fix report contains the covering tests, the command run, and the 670 output; dispatch the re-review once all three are present. That 671 precondition covers the findings the round fixed; a round that declines 672 every finding is defined below. Name the covering test files in the fix 673 message — a one-line fix does not need the whole suite. The per-task loop 674 gives a fix round to an implementer rather than a fixer, so it never uses 675 [fix-subagent-prompt.md](fix-subagent-prompt.md) — that template belongs to 676 the final review's one fix wave. 677 678 **The re-review is scoped.** Run `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` 679 where FIX_BASE is the head the previous review saw, and dispatch 680 [re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) with the findings list, the 681 brief, the report file, and the printed diff path. The re-reviewer verdicts 682 each finding ADDRESSED, NOT ADDRESSED, or DECLINED — a refuted or corrected 683 finding whose file:line evidence the re-reviewer has confirmed; an unconfirmed 684 decline stays NOT ADDRESSED — and flags new breakage in the fix diff only. The 685 controller records each DECLINED finding in the ledger with its evidence. New 686 Critical/Important breakage in the fix diff joins the open findings list. 687 Out-of-scope observations go to the ledger as deferred minors — they never 688 extend the loop. Every round in this loop ends with the scoped re-review — 689 never a full task-reviewer re-run, whatever the finding's origin. 690 691 **A round that declines every finding changes no code.** There is no fix 692 diff and no covering test to confirm; the implementer's report is the 693 artifact, carrying for each finding the refuted or corrected evidence at 694 file:line. Skip `scripts/review-package` for that round — its range is 695 empty — and dispatch the scoped re-review with the findings list, the brief, 696 the report, and the previous review's package path, so the re-reviewer 697 verdicts each finding DECLINED or NOT ADDRESSED from the evidence alone. The 698 covering-tests precondition applies only to findings that were fixed. Record 699 the round as `(0 addressed, declined, open)`; a NOT ADDRESSED verdict 700 keeps that finding open and the round counts toward the cap as usual. 701 702 **After each round,** append to the ledger: 703 `Task : fix round /5 ( addressed, declined, open — ; commits ..)` 704 705 Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays 706 clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review. One narrow 707 exception: a fix fully specified by the finding itself — exact file, exact 708 lines, exact replacement, no judgment left — touching at most 3 lines in 709 one file with no new logic, may be controller-applied — one finding per 710 reach; a round holding two such findings is not de minimis. The exception 711 waives nothing else: it consumes a fix round and ends in the same scoped 712 re-review; the controller applies the edit and runs the fix's covering 713 command FIRST — a failure means the fix was not de minimis: revert the 714 edit, spend no round, and go back to the round's own rule — then commits 715 the verified fix (the re-review packages committed diffs — an 716 uncommitted fix hands it nothing) and appends the fix report — the 717 command, its output, and a diff summary — to the task's report file 718 itself, exactly as an implementer would. Its ledger line keeps the 719 fix-round schema with the marker inside it: 720 `Task : fix round /5 controller-applied (de minimis) ( addressed, declined, open — ; commits ..)`. 721 Reaching for it twice in the same task means the findings are not de 722 minimis — go back to the round's own rule: hand the findings to an 723 implementer at rounds 1-3, dispatch the takeover at rounds 4-5. 724 725 **Codex Review Gate (Claude Code only).** When running under Claude Code, add 726 a Codex **code** review gate at two points — here, per task, and once more 727 at the final whole-branch review — following 728 [../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md](../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md). 729 Probe once per skill run and reuse the result; if Codex is absent, emit the 730 no-Codex notice once and run both gates as no-ops. 731 732 - **Per task:** after the task reviewer approves (spec ✅ and quality approved) and 733 before marking the task complete, run the gate (standard/high effective tiers; an effective-low task skips it per Risk Tiers below, recording the tier-skip event instead) using the per-task code recipe 734 with `--base `. 735 Provide the task brief path, implementer report path, review-package path, and 736 the global-constraints file you wrote in step 3. The gate's dossier `--adjudications` inputs carry the plan's `**Spec:**` file path beside any spec-gate ledger, so the reviewer is handed the binding authority instead of inferring it. 737 - **Rounds are shared, not stacked.** Blocking findings from this gate enter 738 the same five-round loop above, at the next round number — the gate has no 739 separate Codex ceiling of its own. The task's fix-round budget is five, 740 shared across Claude-reviewer rounds and Codex-gate rounds. Three mechanics 741 keep that single budget honest: 742 743 1. **One `GATE_DIR` for this task's whole gate lifecycle.** Create it at 744 the task's first gate invocation and reuse that same dir for every 745 Codex re-round of this task — the gate doc's §3 contract, "Use one 746 `GATE_DIR` for the whole gate." `gate-round`'s counter lives in that 747 dir, so it counts exactly this task's gate rounds and nothing else. 748 When the `GATE_DIR` is first created, record it in the progress ledger 749 as one line `Task N gate dir: `; on resume (or any later Codex 750 re-round), reuse the ledgered path instead of creating a new one; if 751 the ledgered dir no longer exists (cache purged), treat the task's 752 prior gate rounds as unknown and fail closed: do not assume zero — 753 reconstruct the consumed-round count from the ledger's fix-round 754 entries and, if gate rounds cannot be established, surface via BLOCKED 755 rather than restarting the count. 756 2. **Let the counter do the arithmetic.** `gate-round` compares its LOCAL 757 count — gate rounds only, monotonic within the `GATE_DIR` — against a 758 ceiling, so the ceiling must leave gate rounds out; they are already in 759 that count. Pass `--consumed ` (all fix/re-review rounds, whatever the finding's origin — the 761 gate's own invocation rounds are excluded only because `gate-round`'s 762 counter already holds them) and the script derives the ceiling from the 763 shared five-round cap itself. Recompute the consumed count at each call: 764 non-gate rounds may land between gate rounds. Do not hand-compute 765 `--ceiling` for a task gate — that is how twenty measured task gates 766 recorded ceilings of 1, 2, 6, and 7, two of which the cap makes 767 impossible. `--consumed` cannot express them. 768 3. **A spent cap is BLOCKED, not a gate round.** When the task's consumed 769 rounds already total five, `--consumed 5` yields a ceiling of zero and 770 the gate backstops on its first call. That is the fail-closed floor, not 771 the intended path: check before calling, and when the cap is spent follow 772 the breaker below and surface the task as BLOCKED rather than spending a 773 gate invocation to learn it. 774 775 The invariant in one line: **local gate rounds + non-gate fix rounds ≤ 5**, 776 enforced because `gate-round` blocks (verdict `backstop`) the moment its 777 local count would exceed the ceiling. Count every round the 778 gate runs against the task's shared budget — each gate round consumes one 779 of the five, exactly like a reviewer round. After a Codex-triggered fix, 780 the scoped re-review verifies it; the gate re-runs only once that 781 re-review verdicts every finding ADDRESSED or DECLINED. 782 783 **The breaker.** When round 5's re-review — or a per-task Codex gate at the 784 spent cap — still leaves blocking findings open, stop dispatching. The task 785 does not silently continue and nothing is parked on your own authority: 786 surface the open findings to your human partner as BLOCKED, each with the 787 rounds already spent, what was tried, and the evidence. Ledger it: 788 `Task : BLOCKED at cap — `. They decide what happens 789 next. 790 791 ### 5. Complete the task 792 793 When the review comes back clean — the task reviewer approved, every 794 fix-loop finding is addressed or declined, and the per-task Codex gate 795 approved or was skipped by tier — in this order, each step idempotent on a 796 resume: 797 798 - Append `Task : approved ` with the head the reviewers saw, 799 written with `git rev-parse ` (every later approval of the same task 800 appends a new line; the newest is what merges). merge-back compares the 801 whole id, so a shortened id reads as no approval. 802 - Merge back: `scripts/sdd-state merge-back PLAN_FILE N --session --commit `. 803 `merged` continues (`already=1` on a resume means the ref was moved 804 before the crash). `conflict paths=`: merge the integration branch 805 into the task branch in your worktree (`git merge `), resolve 806 through one implementer dispatch whose brief names the paths and both 807 sides, re-run the task reviewer over the resolution and the task gate's 808 re-review lens, append the new `approved` line, and retry. `checked-out` 809 names a worktree or `lease:`: a final train holds the branch; post a 810 `tasks` record and retry after it ends, or ask your human partner to move 811 the checkout. `not-approved approved=` means your bookkeeping 812 is behind: the commit you passed is not the task's newest `approved` line, 813 so append the `approved` line for the head the reviewers saw (or pass that 814 head) and retry. `blocked waiting=` (exit 7) means an amendment put a 815 prerequisite under your claim after you took it, and merge-back enforces 816 the edge: leave the `approved` line as it is, and never write a completion 817 line for a task this session did not complete. Run `next` and take what it 818 offers; on `own-blocked`, post, print the board and hand back as the 819 `own-blocked` text above says. Retry merge-back once every waiting task has 820 its completion line, or after your human partner removes the edge. 821 `not-holder owner=` (exit 4) 822 means the claim is no longer yours (after a takeover your human partner 823 granted, that session holds it): stop and hand back with the line; never 824 repair the ledger or take the claim back. 825 - Detach at the merged head and drop the task branch: 826 `git switch --detach ` then `git branch -d ` 827 (its commits are on the integration branch now; a missing branch on a 828 resume is fine). If `-d` refuses, the branch holds commits that were never 829 approved or merged: keep it, do not force the delete, and hand back to 830 your human partner with git's output. 831 - Complete the task: run `scripts/sdd-state complete PLAN_FILE N 832 --commits ..` and repeat it until it prints `status=complete` 833 (`busy` and `error` are retried; `unknown-task` means the number is not a 834 heading in the plan, `no-workspace` that the ledger is gone, and a usage 835 error that the arguments are wrong: each of those stops you, not the loop). 836 Its `snapshot=` is the completion's durable record. 837 - Mark the todo complete (where you keep todos), and run `next`. 838 839 A task whose ledger has a `merged` line and no completion line is resumed 840 at the completion line, never redispatched. 841 842 ## The waiting board 843 844 Before you ask your human partner a question, hand back BLOCKED, meet an 845 empty frontier (`held` or `blocked`), or stop on a merge conflict, post what 846 you wait on: `scripts/sdd-state wait PLAN_FILE --session --kind 847 [--task N] --note ""`, and put 848 the session lines of `scripts/sdd-state board PLAN_FILE` in what you write. 849 When you resume, clear it: `scripts/sdd-state wait PLAN_FILE --session --clear`. 850 The board is how your human partner finds the session that needs them among 851 several; a session that holds a claim and posts nothing shows as quiet 852 after half an hour, which is where they look for a permission prompt. 853 854 ## Risk Tiers (per-task Codex gate applicability) 855 856 Tiers are `low`, `standard`, `high`, declared per task in the plan. A task 857 skips the per-task Codex gate only when all three hold: declared low, the 858 plan's own Codex gate actually reviewed the plan, and no escalation trigger 859 fired at any point during execution. That skip is recorded durably. An 860 unreviewed low tier — plan gate skipped, degraded, or outcome unknown — 861 executes as standard, and a task demoted that way runs the full train and 862 records NO tier-skip event. The Claude task reviewer and the final 863 whole-branch train never tier off. When any task did skip, write 864 `tier-skips.md` in this plan's workspace; Final Review hands its path to the 865 final reviewer and the final Codex gate. The escalation triggers, the 866 fallback rules, and the exact ledger line shape are in 867 [risk-tiers.md](risk-tiers.md) — read it before dispatching any task declared 868 low. 869 870 ## Final Review 871 872 The final train is claimed. When `next` says `complete`, run 873 `scripts/sdd-state claim PLAN_FILE final --session `: `claimed` means 874 this session runs the final review, the final gate and Finish; `blocked` 875 names tasks still open (claims without completion lines elsewhere: wait or 876 ask); `held` with your own session id (`own=1`, a resume after compaction) 877 means this session already holds the train: continue as its holder; `held` 878 names the session that holds it, or `lease= plan=` 879 when a sibling plan's final holds the branch: post a `tasks` record naming 880 the holder, print the board, and hand back. The holder checks the 881 integration branch out in its own worktree (`git switch `), the 882 one time a session does so, and runs the review package, the final 883 reviewer, the fix wave and the final Codex gate on it; its fix commits land 884 on the integration branch directly, which the lease makes safe. 885 886 Once you hold the train and have checked the integration branch out, the 887 final whole-branch review gets a package too: run 888 `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the 889 branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) — take the path from the 890 `wrote : ...` line and include it in the final review dispatch, so the 891 final reviewer reads one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git 892 commands. Dispatch 893 on the most capable available model (see Model Selection), using 894 hyperpowers:requesting-code-review's 895 [code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at 896 the ledger's deferred-minor lines — and at `tier-skips.md`, if any task 897 skipped its per-task gate — so it can triage which must be fixed before 898 merge. 899 900 If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent 901 with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding. Compose the 902 dispatch from [fix-subagent-prompt.md](fix-subagent-prompt.md). 903 Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real 904 session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined. 905 Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave 906 (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` over the fix range, 907 [re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) using its Final-wave usage note). 908 There is no second fix wave: anything the re-review leaves open — and any 909 finding that conflicts with the plan's text — goes to your human partner 910 with the evidence, as BLOCKED, when finishing-a-development-branch presents 911 the options. 912 913 **Dispatch the decision extractor.** When the ledger has a `Decisions listing:` 914 line (and otherwise nothing), once the fix wave and its re-review are 915 clean (or the final review returned no findings), take a scratch directory 916 from `../requesting-code-review/scripts/codex-review-dir`, regenerate the 917 full-branch package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD`, so a 918 fix wave's commits are in it) and copy it and `/progress.md` into 919 it, and dispatch the 920 extractor in the background, composed from 921 `../finishing-a-development-branch/decision-notes-prompt.md` with those two 922 copies, the plan, the spec, the `Decisions listing:` from the ledger, the 923 index (`decisions/README.md` beside the spec's directory) when it exists, and 924 `/decision-notes.md` as its output path. Record it in the ledger: 925 `Decision extractor: -> /decision-notes.md`. The dispatch is 926 complete only when that line is in the ledger: write it before any other tool 927 call, because after a compaction it is the only record of the task id and the 928 notes path, and without it a resumed controller can neither collect nor stop 929 the extractor. The extractor reads nothing inside the workspace, so Finish may 930 delete the workspace while it runs; 931 finishing-a-development-branch collects it after the full suite and never 932 waits for it, and neither do you. On a harness with no tracked background 933 subagent, skip the dispatch and note it in the ledger. If a Codex final-gate 934 fix changes code after the dispatch: stop the extractor (TaskStop); when the 935 fix altered one of the spec's decisions, settle that first (show your human 936 partner the change you would write into the `## Decisions` item, write and 937 commit it on the branch with their approval; without it the item stands and 938 the change is raised again at the menu); re-run the dry run and replace the 939 ledger's `Decisions listing:`; regenerate the full-branch package and copy 940 it, with the current `/progress.md`, into the scratch directory, 941 replacing the earlier copies; compose the replacement dispatch from those 942 copies; then dispatch the extractor again and replace the 943 `Decision extractor:` line. 944 945 **Codex Review Gate — final whole-branch (Claude Code only).** After the final code-reviewer 946 subagent and its fix wave, and before hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch, 947 run the gate using the final whole-branch code recipe with `--base `. Provide the branch 949 review-package path, plan or requirements path, the Minor findings ledger if 950 present, and the tier-skip summary if any task skipped. The final dossier passes the plan's `**Spec:**` file as a `--doc` input beside the plan, and carries the tier-skip summary among its `--adjudications`. Resolve blocking 951 findings with one fix subagent carrying the complete list, per this 952 section's existing guidance, before finishing. After any Codex-triggered 953 final-review fix, re-run the final code-reviewer before re-running the final 954 Codex gate. 955 956 Unlike the per-task gate, the final gate keeps a ceiling of its own: the 957 gate's convergence stop-rule and per-gate backstop bound this loop (code 958 gates use a code-gate backstop of 3 rounds). If the backstop is hit with 959 unresolved blocking findings, surface them to your human partner rather than 960 looping. 961 962 ## Finish 963 964 When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged: 965 966 1. **Read your session line** from the ledger (its `mode`), and copy the 967 ledger's `Decisions listing:` and `Decision extractor:` lines (or its 968 skip reason) into the hand-off message you are about to send: the next 969 step removes the ledger from the working tree, and 970 hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch takes the mode, the plan, the 971 spec and the extractor's task id and output path as its input. 972 2. **Finish the workspace** with `scripts/sdd-state finish PLAN_FILE --session `: 973 it refuses with `open-claims` while any claimed task lacks a completion line 974 (that is a plan not finished, not a reason for `--force`), and with 975 `busy` (exit 3) when another session is writing the workspace or a copy 976 from an interrupted removal sits beside it (report the stderr line, wait 977 for the other session or ask your human partner about the copy, then run 978 `finish` again); it also refuses with `live-jobs` while a tracked job it 979 names is still live (run `tracked-job wait` on it, or `tracked-job stop` 980 when the job is no longer wanted, then run `finish` again). `not-holder` 981 or `no-final-claim` (exit 11): this session does not hold the final 982 train; stop and hand back. Otherwise it 983 removes the plan's directory, commits the removal to the state branch, 984 and prints `last=`, the commit that still holds the dossier, 985 `push=/` and `receipt=`, the durable copy of the 986 ledger, the guard's log and the job records; record the receipt path in 987 your closing message. A line reading `receipt=none staging=` means 988 the record exists only under that staging path: name the path to your 989 human partner in the closing message. A space in either path prints as 990 `%20`, so decode it before you name the path. On the plain backend it 991 prints `backend=plain` instead of `last=` and `push=`, and there is 992 nothing to push. `none` means there was no workspace to remove, and 993 `error` (exit 2) that the removal or its commit failed: any status other 994 than `finished` stops Finish until the command 995 succeeds; show its stderr line. 996 3. **Verify deletion** with `test ! -d ""` to confirm it is gone. 997 The push command is `git -C push `, the 998 checkout being the parent of the `plans/` directory `sdd-dir` printed; 999 run it only if your human partner asks. 1000 4. **Keep the lease through the branch action.** `finish` leaves the branch 1001 lease in place; hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch marks the 1002 branch closing before a merge and releases the lease after whichever 1003 option your human partner chose. Hand it the plan path and your session 1004 id for that. When the final ends with a hand-back instead, detach your 1005 worktree first (`git switch --detach`) and then release the lease 1006 yourself, as the last action: 1007 `scripts/sdd-state lease PLAN_FILE --release --session `. 1008 1009 A clean finish that leaves the workspace behind is an INCOMPLETE finish — 1010 "keeping it for reference" is not an option; the repo's commits are the 1011 durable record. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them 1012 alone. `scripts/sdd-state prune --repo ` is the only other remover, and it 1013 runs only when asked. 1014 1015 Use hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch, passing the mode from your 1016 session line. Hand it the plan and the spec, and the extractor's task id 1017 and output path when one was dispatched; when the dispatch was skipped, 1018 hand over the ledger's reason instead and say so, and finishing compiles 1019 without notes; when the plan has no spec, say that, and finishing runs its 1020 test-only path. A decision a Codex-gate fix altered was settled in Final 1021 Review before the re-dispatch. 1022 1023 ## Common Rationalizations 1024 1025 The excuses that show up mid-run and what is actually true: 1026 [common-rationalizations.md](common-rationalizations.md). Read it the moment you 1027 catch yourself justifying a shortcut. 1028 1029 ## Example Workflow 1030 1031 A complete worked run, dispatch through finish: 1032 [example-workflow.md](example-workflow.md). 1033
